Development Maya · Newborn 2 mo Your guide 4 mo 6 mo 9 mo 12 mo First looks and smiles Look for small responses to you: watching your face, calming to your voice and smiling back. Social How baby connects with you and others Settles with your voice or touch › Looks at your face › Seems glad to see you › Smiles back at you › Communication Sounds, gestures and first words Makes sounds beyond crying › Responds to loud sounds › Thinking How baby explores and figures things out Watches you move › Looks at a toy for a few seconds › Movement How baby moves their body Lifts head during tummy time › Moves both arms and legs › Briefly opens hands › Looking ahead: most babies show these skills by 2 months. They can emerge earlier; not all are expected during the newborn stage. Common questions Do I need to save every skill? ＋ No. Guidance stays available without saving anything. Save the moments you want to remember; an unsaved skill doesn’t mean it’s missing. When should I ask our pediatrician about a skill? ＋ If baby isn’t showing one or more skills by the guide’s reference age, loses a skill or something concerns you, tell your pediatrician. You don’t need to wait for the next checkup. See CDC photos and videos By 2 months ↗ Sources behind this guide ＋ Adapted from CDC’s Learn the Signs. Act Early. Sleep Maya · Newborn Newborn sleep Your guide Day and night sleep Naps and bedtime Two naps Recommended for this age Newborn sleep: around the clock Short sleeps of 1–3 hours, day and night, with feeds in between. No pattern yet, and that’s expected. Safe sleep setup 0 of 6 checked Back to sleep, a clear crib in your room, and never on a sofa. Open checklist → Why it’s happening Baby’s body clock hasn’t switched on yet, so day and night feel the same. Hunger sets the pace. Sleep at a glance Awake time is the stretch between sleeps. Total 14–17 h Naps Many Awake 45–60 min Bedtime Varies Typical range · Includes naps A day follows a loop: feed, a short awake time, then sleep. Repeat through the night; there is no clock-time schedule yet. This repeats day and night. Most of the awake time is feeding. At night Wake baby to feed until your pediatrician says you can stop, usually once birth weight is back. What helps Start settling at the first yawn Watch for a quieter gaze, turning away or yawning. Try settling when these appear; the awake-time range is a starting point, not a timer. Help baby fall asleep Feeding, rocking or holding baby to sleep is normal and fine now. Take turns overnight If another adult can help, agree who will handle each stretch. They can change, settle or bring baby for feeds so you can rest between them. Call your pediatrician if Baby is hard to wake for feeds, or has a temperature of 100.4°F or higher. → Common questions right now Why won’t she settle? ＋ Is she fed and changed? Yes, still fussing Not sure Why are evenings so hard? ＋ Is it mostly late afternoon and evening? Yes It’s all day Is it OK that she only naps on me? ＋ Does she sleep in her own space at night? Yes, just not naps No, only on me Coming up · Usually 6 weeks–3 months Day and night sleep One stretch of 3–5 hours at night. Feeding Maya · Newborn Newborn feeding Your guide Changing milk feeds Getting ready for solids Starting solids Textures and finger foods Family meals Recommended for this age Newborn feeding: little and often Feeds come often, day and night, while you and baby figure it out together. Small, frequent feeds are exactly right. If you’re nursing Ask about vitamin D drops Breastfed and partly breastfed babies need vitamin D drops every day, starting in the first days. See milk basics → Why it’s happening Newborns need frequent feeds as they grow. If you’re nursing, feeding often also helps build your milk supply. How much and how often A guide, not a target. Milk reference Nursing Breast-milk bottles Formula bottles Nursing and bottles Total milk feeds 8–12 Nursing Every 1–3 hours Formula-only bottle 1–2 oz, then 2–3 oz by 2 weeks How to tell it’s enough At least 6 wet diapers a day after day 5, and back to birth weight by about 2 weeks. What helps What feeding on demand looks like Offer milk at hunger cues—even if baby fed an hour ago. Rooting, lip smacking and hands to mouth can come before crying. Let her end the feed Turning away, slowing down or closing her mouth can mean she has had enough. Sleepiness alone doesn’t tell you she took enough milk. She doesn’t need to finish a bottle. Get help early if nursing hurts Pain past the first few seconds, or trouble latching, is worth a lactation visit now. Call your pediatrician if Baby is hard to wake for feeds, skin or eyes look more yellow, or wet diapers are fewer than expected for the day of life. After day 5, expect at least 6 wet diapers a day. → Also common around now Cluster feeding and growth spurts Often around 3 weeks, 6 weeks and 3 months. Suddenly feeding much more often, especially in the evening. → Common questions right now Do I need to wake her to feed? ＋ Is she back to her birth weight? Not yet, or not sure Yes, and gaining well Can I give her water? ＋ Is it hot out? Yes, I’m worried she is thirsty Just wondering Spit-up, gas or hiccups: is this normal? ＋ How does she seem after feeds? Happy and growing Upset, arching or not gaining Coming up · Usually 6 weeks–4 months Changing milk feeds Milk feeds may become more efficient; longer night stretches are not required. Safety Maya · Newborn First setup Your guide Reaching and rolling Before crawling Crawling and scooting Before pulling up Your first safety setup Check the car seat, hot water, alarms and any pool access. Your checklist 4 left Check the car-seat fit and installation A certified technician can check the installation and show you the harness fit. How to check ＋ For a rear-facing seat, harness straps sit at or below baby’s shoulders, and you can’t pinch any slack at the shoulder. The chest clip sits at armpit level. Follow your seat and vehicle manuals. NHTSA · Car-seat checks ↗ Find a certified installation check ↗ Doesn’t apply Check the hot-water setting Set the water heater to 120°F or lower. How to check ＋ Follow the heater instructions, or ask a plumber or your landlord. Check bath water and stay within reach; a lower setting does not replace supervision. Anti-scald devices add protection at taps. CPSC · See the guidance ↗ Doesn’t apply Check smoke and carbon monoxide alarms Test each alarm and check placement, including the areas around baby’s bedroom. How to check ＋ Smoke alarms belong on every level, inside bedrooms and outside sleeping areas. Put CO alarms near sleeping areas and follow manufacturer instructions for testing and replacement. CPSC · See the guidance ↗ Doesn’t apply 1 more check ＋ Secure pool or spa access Use barriers and self-closing, self-latching gates that separate children from the water. How to check ＋ Check doors leading outside too, and close gates after every use. Barriers don’t replace watching baby near water. CPSC Pool Safely · Barriers & supervision ↗ Doesn’t apply Coming up Before reaching and rolling Check what’s within reach, the floor around the play mat and your changing spot. See the checklist → Sources behind this checklist ＋ Based on CPSC home-safety guidance, with AAP guidance on household hazards and NHTSA guidance on car seats. Play & everyday activities Maya · Newborn Newborn Your guide 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo Newborn · Play Face to face A pause after your smile gives baby time to answer with a look or a wiggle. What you’ll need No toys needed; a comfortable place to hold baby. How to play Hold baby close with their head supported. Smile, then pause so they can look at you. What to notice A brief look toward your face can be their turn; a smile isn’t required. Make it easier Try while baby lies comfortably on their back if being held feels too busy. If they want more Copy a small expression baby makes, then wait. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. Play & everyday activities Maya · Newborn Newborn Your guide 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo Newborn · Play A song and a slow sway A familiar voice and a repeating rhythm give baby something predictable to listen to. What you’ll need Your voice and a comfortable place to stand or sit. How to play Support baby’s head and body against you and gently sway while singing one short song. What to notice Baby may look toward you or settle against you. Quiet listening counts too. Make it easier Stay still and sing softly if movement isn’t welcome. If they want more Repeat one line, leaving a little pause before singing it again. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. ← Previous idea Next: Tummy time with you → Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Play through the first year ↗ AAP · Play, interaction and developing skills ↗ AAP · Play with everyday objects ↗ Illustrations are simplified examples.

Play & everyday activities Maya · Newborn Newborn Your guide 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo Newborn · Play Tummy time with you Your face gives baby a reason to lift their head, for just a moment at a time. What you’ll need A comfortable reclined position while you are fully awake. How to play While you are awake and reclined, place baby on your chest for supervised tummy time. Talk where they can see you. What to notice A small head lift or turn toward your voice is enough; rest their head when they need a break. Make it easier Try a very brief turn and stop when baby has had enough. If they want more Move your face slightly to one side and wait for their interest. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. ← Previous idea Next: One bold picture → Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Play through the first year ↗ AAP · Play, interaction and developing skills ↗ AAP · Play with everyday objects ↗ Illustrations are simplified examples.

Play & everyday activities Maya · Newborn Newborn Your guide 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo Newborn · Play One bold picture Keeping the picture still gives baby time to focus before anything changes. What you’ll need One high-contrast baby picture or board-book page. How to play Hold a high-contrast picture near baby’s face while they are awake. Keep it still and let them look. What to notice Their eyes may settle on the picture for a moment, then look away. Make it easier Use your face instead if the picture doesn’t interest them. If they want more Slowly move it a small distance and see whether their gaze follows. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. ← Previous idea Next: A tiny tour of home → Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Play through the first year ↗ AAP · Play, interaction and developing skills ↗ AAP · Play with everyday objects ↗ Illustrations are simplified examples.

Play & everyday activities Maya · Newborn Newborn Your guide 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo Newborn · Play A tiny tour of home Naming one thing while you both look connects a word, a voice and a place. What you’ll need A window or picture to stop beside; no special toys. How to play Carry baby with their head supported. Stop by one window or picture and describe what you see. What to notice A look toward the window or a pause in movement can be a response. Make it easier Stay in one comfortable spot and describe what is nearby. If they want more Return to the same spot later and use the same simple words. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. ← Previous idea Next: A rhyme in your arms → Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Play through the first year ↗ AAP · Play, interaction and developing skills ↗ AAP · Play with everyday objects ↗ Illustrations are simplified examples.

Play & everyday activities Maya · Newborn Newborn Your guide 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo Newborn · Play A rhyme in your arms The rise and fall of your voice makes everyday language interesting to hear. What you’ll need A comfortable hold and a short rhyme you remember. How to play Hold baby comfortably and say a short rhyme in a gentle, rhythmic voice. Pause between lines. What to notice Baby might watch your mouth, move or simply listen. Make it easier Whisper just one line if they seem sensitive to sound. If they want more Leave a pause at the end of a familiar line before repeating it. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. ← Previous idea Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Play through the first year ↗ AAP · Play, interaction and developing skills ↗ AAP · Play with everyday objects ↗ Illustrations are simplified examples.

Play & everyday activities Maya · 1 month Newborn 1 mo Your guide 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo 1 mo · Play Try a new expression Changing one expression at a time makes a social exchange easier to follow. What you’ll need No toys; a position where baby can see your face. How to play With baby facing you, slowly open your mouth or lift your eyebrows. Wait and watch their reaction. What to notice They might watch closely, open their mouth or move their eyebrows; copying isn’t necessary. Make it easier Keep to a smile if bigger expressions seem startling. If they want more Copy their expression instead and let them lead the exchange. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. Play & everyday activities Maya · 1 month Newborn 1 mo Your guide 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo 1 mo · Play Meet me on the floor Your face at floor level makes looking up part of being together. What you’ll need A firm floor mat with space for you to lie beside baby. How to play During supervised tummy time on a firm floor mat, lie facing baby and talk at their eye level. What to notice Notice a brief lift or a turn toward your voice, with rests between efforts. Make it easier Bring your face closer rather than asking baby to lift higher. If they want more Sing one short line from their eye level and pause for a response. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. ← Previous idea Next: Answer their little sounds → Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Play through the first year ↗ AAP · Play, interaction and developing skills ↗ AAP · Play with everyday objects ↗ Illustrations are simplified examples.

Play & everyday activities Maya · 1 month Newborn 1 mo Your guide 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo 1 mo · Play Answer their little sounds Taking turns with sounds introduces the rhythm of a conversation before words. What you’ll need No equipment; a quiet moment when baby is alert. How to play When baby makes a sound, answer it once. Then wait quietly for a look, movement or sound back. What to notice A look, kick or another little sound can be their reply. Make it easier Respond to a facial expression if baby isn’t making sounds. If they want more Copy a new sound they choose rather than asking for a particular one. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. ← Previous idea Next: A book with two voices → Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Play through the first year ↗ AAP · Play, interaction and developing skills ↗ AAP · Play with everyday objects ↗ Illustrations are simplified examples.

What you’ll need A picture book and a comfortable supported hold. How to play Read a few lines while holding baby comfortably. Try a slightly different voice for each character. What to notice They may look toward your mouth or become still as you change voices. Make it easier Use one calm voice if changing voices feels too exciting. If they want more Pause on one picture and add a short sound for it. Stay with baby during play. Play & everyday activities Maya · 1 month Newborn 1 mo Your guide 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo 1 mo · Play Listen by the window Sharing one sound helps baby notice it without a busy stream of new things. What you’ll need A comfortable spot by a window. How to play Hold baby comfortably near a window. Name a bird, leaves or another sound, then pause to listen. What to notice They may become quiet, move their eyes or turn toward the sound. Make it easier Try a quieter room if outside sounds are overwhelming. Play & everyday activities Maya · 5 months Newborn 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo Your guide 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo 5 mo · Play Hello, little feet Seeing and feeling their feet helps baby learn how their body moves. What you’ll need A firm floor mat; no toys needed. How to play During back play on a firm floor mat, touch and name baby’s feet. Pause to let them look, kick or reach toward them. What to notice They may look down, kick, reach or simply watch your hand touch a foot. Make it easier Let baby watch your hand touching one foot; don’t pull their legs into position. If they want more Pause after naming one foot and follow the movement baby chooses. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. Play & everyday activities Maya · 5 months Newborn 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo Your guide 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo 5 mo · Play A reason to turn A nearby toy gives looking, reaching and turning the same interesting destination. What you’ll need A firm floor mat and one favorite baby-safe toy. How to play On a firm floor mat, show baby a favorite toy, then hold it slightly to one side. Let them decide whether to look, reach or turn. What to notice Looking or reaching toward the toy counts. They don't need to complete a roll. Make it easier Keep the toy close. Looking or reaching is enough; don’t pull baby into a roll. If they want more Offer the toy on the other side during a later turn, keeping it easy to reach. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. ← Previous idea Next: Where’s that gentle sound? → Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Play through the first year ↗ AAP · Play, interaction and developing skills ↗ AAP · Play with everyday objects ↗ Illustrations are simplified examples.

Play & everyday activities Maya · 5 months Newborn 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo Your guide 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo 5 mo · Play Where’s that gentle sound? A visible sound source brings listening and looking into the same game. What you’ll need A softly sounding one-piece baby rattle. How to play While baby is comfortably supported, softly shake a baby rattle just to one side, where they can also see it. Wait for their response. What to notice Baby may move their eyes before turning their head, or keep watching the rattle. Make it easier Bring it in front if baby doesn’t turn. This is a game, not a hearing test. If they want more Pause the sound, then make it once more and wait. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. ← Previous idea Next: Smooth or bumpy? → Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Play through the first year ↗ AAP · Play, interaction and developing skills ↗ AAP · Play with everyday objects ↗ Illustrations are simplified examples.

Play & everyday activities Maya · 5 months Newborn 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo Your guide 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo 5 mo · Play Smooth or bumpy? Exploring one surface and then another gives hands something to compare. What you’ll need Two intact baby-safe toys with different surfaces. How to play Offer two intact baby-safe toys with different surfaces, one at a time. Let baby hold and explore each. What to notice They may grip, rub or mouth a toy, or keep choosing one over the other. Make it easier Use one toy and let baby explore without switching. If they want more Offer the two toys where both can be seen and follow their choice. Stay with baby during play. Play & everyday activities Maya · 5 months Newborn 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo Your guide 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo 5 mo · Play A little peekaboo A familiar face disappearing briefly and returning makes a predictable social game. What you’ll need Just your hands and face. How to play Cover your own face with your hands, then open them and say “peekaboo.” Keep your voice gentle and watch baby’s reaction. What to notice A look, kick, smile or still attention can be their response; laughter isn’t required. Make it easier Hide just your eyes if the full reveal seems startling. If they want more Pause just before the reveal and let their interest set the pace. Stay with baby during play. What you’ll need A sturdy picture book; your rhyme can be only two words. How to play Share a board book and make up a short rhyme about one picture. Repeat the rhythm and leave a pause. What to notice They might look at the picture, pat the page or make a sound in the pause. Make it easier Use two simple words rather than a whole rhyme. If they want more Use the same rhyme when that picture appears another time. Stay with baby during play. Milk reference Nursing Breast-milk bottles Formula bottles Nursing and bottles Nursing On demand, still the main food Bottles Amounts depend on how much baby nurses; follow hunger and fullness cues. Safety Maya · 6 months First setup Reaching and rolling Before crawling Your guide Crawling and scooting Before pulling up Prepare before scooting or crawling Your babyproofing checklist Work through the rooms baby will use, including the furniture and windows they may reach next. Your checklist 8 left Fit the right stair gates Gate the top and bottom of stairs. At the top, use a gate screwed into the wall, not a pressure-mounted or pet gate. How to check ＋ Use a gate made for children and follow its instructions. Check doorways into rooms baby shouldn’t enter, too. CPSC · Gate guidance ↗ Doesn’t apply Anchor furniture and TVs Secure dressers, bookcases and TVs before baby uses them as handholds. How to check ＋ Use anti-tip hardware suited to your furniture and wall. Follow the hardware and furniture instructions; the guide shows how to attach and check it. CPSC · Anchor It ↗ Doesn’t apply Lock away medicines and cleaning products Lock away cleaners, detergent pods, medicines, vitamins and supplements, even in child-resistant packaging. How to check ＋ Relock after each use and pull the door to check it holds. AAP · What to lock away ↗ US Poison Control · 1-800-222-1222 Doesn’t apply 5 more checks ＋ Cover outlets and move cords Use outlet covers baby can’t pull out, and move cords out of reach. How to check ＋ Choose covers baby cannot remove and that are too large to choke on. If replacing outlets, use tamper-resistant ones. CPSC · See the guidance ↗ Doesn’t apply Check window access Move furniture baby could climb away from windows. Screens don’t stop falls. How to check ＋ Use window stops or guards to limit openings and gaps to 4 inches or less. Keep at least one window in each room usable by an adult for escape in a fire. CPSC · Window guidance ↗ Doesn’t apply Go cordless on window coverings Choose cordless blinds or shades. Check for cords reachable from the floor and from furniture. How to check ＋ Inner cords and loops can be reachable even when the pull cord is tied up. AAP · Window-covering safety ↗ Doesn’t apply Keep bathrooms and other risky rooms closed off Use suitable latches, knob covers or gates to block access to bathrooms, the laundry room and garage. How to check ＋ Choose devices adults can open quickly in an emergency. Check toilet and water access; consider a toilet-lid lock. Relatch doors after use. CPSC · See the guidance ↗ Doesn’t apply Skip seated walkers with wheels They let baby move fast and reach hazards, and they don’t help with walking. How to check ＋ Choose floor play or a stationary activity center instead. This advice is about seated walkers with wheels; push-along toys are a different product. What you’ll need One light, easy-to-grasp baby toy. How to play Offer one light, easy-to-grasp baby toy at the center of baby’s body. Let them hold it, turn it or move it between hands. What to notice Holding it with both hands, or touching it with the second hand, counts. Passing it between hands isn’t required. What you’ll need A firm floor mat, one baby-safe toy and your hands to steady them. How to play During floor play, support baby around their chest and waist as needed. AAP · Window-covering safety ↗ Doesn’t apply Keep bathrooms and other risky rooms closed off Use suitable latches, knob covers or gates to block access to bathrooms, the laundry room and garage. How to check ＋ Choose devices adults can open quickly in an emergency. Check toilet and water access; consider a toilet-lid lock. Relatch doors after use. CPSC · See the guidance ↗ Doesn’t apply Skip seated walkers with wheels They let baby move fast and reach hazards, and they don’t help with walking. How to check ＋ Choose floor play or a stationary activity center instead. This advice is about seated walkers with wheels; push-along toys are a different product. Play & everyday activities Maya · 12 months Newborn 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo Your guide 12 mo · Play A pretend sip Copying a pretend sip brings a familiar routine into make-believe. What you’ll need An empty baby-safe cup; a second cup if you want your own. How to play Pretend to drink from an empty baby-safe cup. Offer it for baby to explore or copy, with no need to add liquid. What to notice They may turn the cup, bring it toward their face or watch you sip. Make it easier Let baby hold and turn the cup while you pretend with another. If they want more Offer a pretend sip to a baby-safe soft toy while baby watches. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. Play & everyday activities Maya · 12 months Newborn 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo Your guide 12 mo · Play Pour a little water Tipping a cup makes water move, giving grasping and turning an immediate result. What you’ll need A shallow bowl, two sturdy cups, a little lukewarm water and a washable spot. How to play Sit beside baby with a shallow bowl, two sturdy cups and a little lukewarm water. Show water pouring from a cup into the bowl, then offer a turn with your help. Stay within arm’s reach and empty the bowl when play ends. What to notice Baby may splash, hold the cup or watch you pour. Independent pouring is not required. Make it easier Hold the cup together if baby welcomes help, or explore an empty cup first. If they want more Help baby scoop a little water back into the cup, then tip it into the bowl again. Stay with baby during play. Pause when they turn away, fuss or seem tired. ← Previous idea Next: Sing about hands and feet → Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Play through the first year ↗ AAP · Play, interaction and developing skills ↗ AAP · Play with everyday objects ↗ Illustrations are simplified examples.

Play & everyday activities Maya · 12 months Newborn 1 mo 2 mo 3 mo 4 mo 5 mo 6 mo 7 mo 8 mo 9 mo 10 mo 11 mo 12 mo Your guide 12 mo · Play Help me hide it Choosing a hiding spot adds a new role to an already familiar finding game. What you’ll need A large baby-safe toy and a low open basket. How to play Let baby watch you hide a large toy behind a low open basket. Invite them to find it, then offer a turn placing the toy there. What to notice They may put the toy beside the basket or watch you hide it. Make it easier Keep part of the toy visible and do the hiding yourself. If they want more Swap roles: look for the toy wherever baby has placed it. Stay with baby during play. Total 14–17 h Naps Many Awake 45–60 min Bedtime Varies Typical range · Includes naps A day follows a loop: feed, a short awake time, then sleep. Repeat through the night; there is no clock-time schedule yet. This repeats day and night. Most of the awake time is feeding. Try settling when these appear; the awake-time range is a starting point, not a timer. Help baby fall asleep Feeding, rocking or holding baby to sleep is normal and fine now. Take turns overnight If another adult can help, agree who will handle each stretch. They can change, settle or bring baby for feeds so you can rest between them. Sleep Maya · 5 months Newborn sleep Day and night sleep Naps and bedtime Your guide Two naps Usually 3–5 months The 4-month sleep regression Around 4 months, sleep cycles mature. Some babies wake more often or have shorter naps during this change; others have no obvious disruption. What you might notice More night waking than a few weeks ago Naps that end after 30–45 minutes Harder to put down asleep Why it’s happening Sleep cycles are maturing. Baby may wake more fully between cycles and need help returning to sleep. How long it lasts The disruption varies. If waking persists or comes with feeding or health concerns, review the pattern with your pediatrician. What helps Keep one familiar settling sequence Use the same short wind-down and settling help. Respond to hunger or discomfort; you do not need to introduce sleep training to handle this change. After a short nap, offer the next one sooner Watch for tired signs rather than waiting for the usual time. Keep in mind Keep needed night feeds. Sleep Maya · 5 months Newborn sleep Day and night sleep Naps and bedtime Your guide Two naps Usually 8–10 months Separation anxiety Sometimes called the 8-month sleep regression. Baby may protest when you leave, including at bedtime and during the night. What you might notice Crying as soon as you walk out Waking and looking for you Wanting the same parent every night Why it’s happening Awareness of familiar people and being apart is growing. Baby may seek more reassurance when you leave, including at bedtime. How long it lasts It comes and goes. It often peaks around 9–10 months and can return in the second year. What helps Use the same short goodbye Something like “I love you. Time to sleep.” Predictable works better than sneaking out. Use familiar reassurance Respond with the comfort that fits your approach: your voice, a brief visit or more help settling. Keep the bedtime sequence familiar. Keep in mind Keep the usual nap pattern; harder goodbyes alone do not mean a nap should go. content.question: Why won’t she settle?
content.prompt: Is she fed and changed?
content.action: Try one way of soothing at a time for a few minutes: holding, rocking, shushing or a song. Switching fast can make it harder.
content.context: Newborns often need help to fall asleep. That’s normal now.

content.question: Why won’t she settle?
content.prompt: Is she fed and changed?
content.action: Look for hunger cues and offer a feed if baby seems hungry. Also check diaper comfort and whether baby needs help settling.
content.context: Rooting and hands to the mouth are hunger signs.

content.question: Why are evenings so hard?
content.prompt: Is it mostly late afternoon and evening?
content.action: Evening fussiness is very common. Dim the lights, cut the noise and feed as often as she wants.
content.context: It often peaks around 6 weeks and eases by 3–4 months.

content.question: Why are evenings so hard?
content.prompt: Is it mostly late afternoon and evening?
content.action: Long, hard-to-soothe crying through the day is worth a call to your pediatrician.
content.context: Call right away if it comes with fever, vomiting or poor feeding.

content.question: Is it OK that she only naps on me?
content.prompt: Does she sleep in her own space at night?
content.action: If you hold baby for a nap, stay fully awake. You can also try settling for one nap in their own flat, firm sleep space.
content.context: Crib naps can still be short. A wake-up during transfer does not mean you need to change the whole routine.

content.question: Is it OK that she only naps on me?
content.prompt: Does she sleep in her own space at night?
content.action: Try transferring baby gently to their own flat, firm sleep space after settling. If they wake, soothe and try again; there is no required transfer time.
content.context: If you’re getting sleepy, put her down first, even if she wakes.

content.question: Why won’t she settle for naps?
content.prompt: What do you notice when you try?
content.action: Try a quieter, darker room and the settling help that usually works. Next time, start winding down before baby becomes upset.
content.context: Overtired babies often fight sleep harder.

content.question: Why is she fighting the catnap?
content.prompt: How does she do without it?
content.action: She may be starting the 3-to-2 nap transition. On days she skips it, move bedtime earlier.
content.context: Look for a repeated pattern of managing comfortably until bedtime, rather than deciding from one skipped nap.

content.question: Why is she fighting the catnap?
content.prompt: How does she do without it?
content.action: Offer another nap with the settling help that usually works, using a safe sleep space. If the nap does not happen, bring bedtime earlier.
content.context: A car seat or swing is not a substitute for a flat, firm sleep space at home.

content.question: Why is she waking more at night?
content.prompt: Has anything changed recently?
content.action: Practice the skill in the day. New skills often show up at night for a week or two.
content.context: Place baby on their back for every sleep. If baby comfortably rolls both ways, you do not need to keep turning them back. Keep the sleep space clear.

content.question: Why is she waking more at night?
content.prompt: Has anything changed recently?
content.action: Check feeding needs, discomfort and recent changes before changing the routine. Keep the familiar bedtime sequence and note when the waking happens.
content.context: If waking comes with fever or poor feeding, call your pediatrician.

content.question: Why is bedtime suddenly harder?
content.prompt: When did the afternoon nap end?
content.action: If baby is still alert, try bedtime 15–30 minutes later tonight. See whether late naps keep pushing bedtime back before changing the nap routine.
content.context: Compare the last awake stretch with the range above and how tired baby seems; one difficult bedtime does not establish a new pattern.

content.question: Why is bedtime suddenly harder?
content.prompt: When did the afternoon nap end?
content.action: If baby protests when you leave, try a familiar short goodbye and your usual reassurance. Also check hunger, discomfort and whether bedtime still fits the day.
content.context: Harder goodbyes can come and go; they do not automatically mean the routine has stopped working.

content.question: Why is she waking more at night?
content.prompt: Anything new lately?
content.action: Offer the comfort she needs now. Go back to your usual routine once she’s better.
content.context: Call your pediatrician if waking comes with fever, poor feeding or signs of pain. Ear pulling alone does not establish an ear infection.

content.question: Why is she waking more at night?
content.prompt: Anything new lately?
content.action: Help her lie down calmly, and practice sitting down from standing during play.
content.context: Offer practice while awake; new skills may need time before they feel easy at night.

content.question: Why is she waking more at night?
content.prompt: Anything new lately?
content.choice: None of these, or not sure
content.action: Note bedtime, naps, wakes and feeds for a few nights. Check hunger and discomfort, then change one part of the routine at a time if a pattern emerges.
content.context: Snoring most nights, pauses in breathing or ongoing feeding or growth concerns deserve a pediatrician review.

content.question: Why is she up so early?
content.prompt: What time is bedtime?
content.action: Try bedtime 15–30 minutes earlier. Overtired babies often wake earlier, not later.
content.context: If baby is comfortable, watch the pattern over a few days rather than deciding from one early wake.

content.question: Why is she up so early?
content.prompt: What time is bedtime?
content.action: Keep early waking quiet and dim while responding to hunger or discomfort. Choose a consistent morning start when baby can comfortably manage it.
content.context: A morning nap that starts too early can keep early waking going.

content.question: Why is she up so early?
content.prompt: What time is bedtime?
content.action: Look at the whole pattern: when the last nap ends, how tired baby is at bedtime and whether dawn light wakes them. Change one thing at a time.
content.context: Respond to feeding and comfort needs; an early wake alone does not show which part of the routine needs changing.

units.content: Sleep Maya · 5 months Safe sleep Safe sleep setup Set this up once, before birth or in the first days. It applies to every nap and every night, whichever way you settle baby. Your setup 6 left Back to sleep, every sleep On their back, on a firm, flat crib or bassinet mattress with only a fitted sheet. No pillows, bumpers, blankets or toys. Same room, separate sleep space Keep the crib or bassinet in your room for at least the first 6 months. Never sleep with baby on a sofa or armchair It’s the most dangerous place to fall asleep with a baby. If you might doze while feeding, an adult bed cleared of pillows and blankets is less risky. Move baby back to their own space when you wake. Use a flat sleep space outside travel Use the car seat for travel. At your destination, move a sleeping baby to their own flat, firm sleep space. Swings are not routine sleep spaces. Keep baby from overheating One more light layer than you’d wear. No hats, and no weighted sleep sacks or swaddles. Offer a pacifier at sleep times Once feeding is going well. It’s linked to lower SIDS risk. If it falls out, you don’t need to put it back. As baby grows When baby tries to roll Stop swaddling. Use sleepwear or a sleep sack that leaves arms free. Keep placing baby on her back; once she rolls both ways, you can leave her. Before baby can sit Lower the crib mattress before baby can sit. Follow the crib manual for the right position. Before baby can pull up Set the mattress to its lowest and remove mobiles and anything she can reach. Moving to her own room Room-sharing is recommended for at least the first 6 months. After that, when to move is up to you. Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · A parent’s guide to safe sleep ↗ AAP · When to stop swaddling ↗ AAP · Crib height and room safety ↗ AAP · Getting your baby to sleep ↗ AAP · Separation anxiety and sleep ↗ Based on AAP safe sleep guidance, 2022.

Sleep Maya · 5 months Sleep When to ask for sleep help How to tell Normal Waking at night through the first year. Short naps while sleep patterns develop. Keep an eye on it Note a pattern of harder settling or more waking, including feeds and any signs of discomfort. Call your pediatrician if Snoring most nights or pauses and gasping during sleep. Sleep changes with fever or poor feeding. A newborn who is hard to wake for feeds. Call 911 if Trouble breathing, blue or gray lips, or baby won’t wake up. For you Look after yourself too If exhaustion or low mood is getting hard to manage, talk to your own doctor, or call or text the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline: 1-833-852-6262. Before a visit, note a few nights of bedtime, wakes and feeds. It helps your pediatrician see the pattern.

Feeding Maya · 5 months Newborn feeding Changing milk feeds Getting ready for solids Your guide Starting solids Textures and finger foods Family meals Earlier · Birth–6 weeks Newborn feeding: little and often Feeds come often, day and night, while you and baby figure it out together. Small, frequent feeds are exactly right. ← Back to your guide Why it’s happening Newborns need frequent feeds as they grow. If you’re nursing, feeding often also helps build your milk supply. How much and how often A guide, not a target. Milk reference Nursing Breast-milk bottles Formula bottles Nursing and bottles Total milk feeds 8–12 Nursing Every 1–3 hours Formula-only bottle 1–2 oz, then 2–3 oz by 2 weeks How to tell it’s enough At least 6 wet diapers a day after day 5, and back to birth weight by about 2 weeks. What helps What feeding on demand looks like Offer milk at hunger cues—even if baby fed an hour ago. Rooting, lip smacking and hands to mouth can come before crying. Let her end the feed Turning away, slowing down or closing her mouth can mean she has had enough. Sleepiness alone doesn’t tell you she took enough milk. She doesn’t need to finish a bottle. Get help early if nursing hurts Pain past the first few seconds, or trouble latching, is worth a lactation visit now. Call your pediatrician if Baby is hard to wake for feeds, skin or eyes look more yellow, or wet diapers are fewer than expected for the day of life. After day 5, expect at least 6 wet diapers a day. → Common questions at this stage Do I need to wake her to feed? ＋ Is she back to her birth weight? Feeds may become shorter or further apart, with hungrier days in between. Watch intake and growth rather than expecting a fixed schedule. ← Back to your guide Why it’s happening Some babies take milk more efficiently as they grow. Shorter feeds alone don’t tell you how much milk she is getting; growth and wet diapers help show the overall pattern. How much and how often A guide, not a target. Milk reference Nursing Breast-milk bottles Formula bottles Nursing and bottles Total milk feeds 6–8 Nursing Every 2–4 hours Formula-only bottle 4–5 oz every 3–4 hours Growth spurts can bring back frequent feeds for a few days. How to tell it’s enough Steady growth along her own curve at checkups, and regular wet diapers. What helps Follow her cues, not the clock Offer milk at hunger cues and pause at fullness cues. A hungrier day does not mean the usual pattern has failed. Pace bottle feeds Hold the bottle more level and pause every few minutes so she can decide when she is full. Never prop a bottle. Keep usual milk feeds while you prepare. Before the first bite 0 of 4 ready High chair, choking first aid and a few basics. Set up before solids start. Open checklist → Why it’s happening Breast milk or formula stays the main nutrition while head control, sitting and swallowing skills develop. Around 6 months is a common starting point, alongside readiness signs. How much and how often A guide, not a target. Milk reference Nursing Breast-milk bottles Formula bottles Nursing and bottles Total milk feeds 5–7 Nursing Every 3–4 hours Formula-only bottle 4–6 oz A hungrier day is a reason to offer milk and follow feeding cues. It is not a readiness sign for solids. How to tell it’s enough Steady growth and regular wet diapers. What helps Watch for the readiness signs Steady head, sits with support, opens for offered food, and swallows instead of pushing food out. Watching you eat isn’t a sign on its own. Also common around now Distracted feeding Usually 4–6 months. Pulling off to look around during most feeds. → Common questions right now She seems hungrier. Should we start solids early? ＋ Has your pediatrician suggested starting early? Yes No, she just seems hungry Purées or baby-led weaning? ＋ Purées You offer small spoonfuls and can adjust the texture yourself. This takes your help for each bite; move toward mashed and lumpier foods as baby learns. Baby-led weaning Baby brings prepared finger foods to their mouth. Choose this if you feel comfortable preparing safe shapes and letting baby explore, including dropped food and mess. Milk feeds continue. A mix of both Offer some foods by spoon and some as soft finger foods, even at the same meal. You do not need to choose one approach permanently. Readiness and safe food preparation matter in every approach. Baby decides how much to eat. Start with manageable food and keep usual milk feeds alongside. Already started solids? Update your guide ← Back to your guide Why it’s happening Around 6 months, iron-rich foods become an important part of the diet alongside milk. Early introduction of peanut and well-cooked egg may help prevent those allergies. How much and how often A guide, not a target. How to tell it’s enough Milk still carries her growth. At meals, watch her interest and fullness, not how much she eats. What helps Offer iron in a form baby can manage Try mashed beans, iron-fortified infant cereal mixed with breast milk or formula, or soft shredded meat. You can offer a spoonful or let baby hold the loaded spoon; safely prepared finger foods can fit alongside. Introduce peanut and egg early Offer them in a safe form, then keep them in her diet. See Introducing allergens for how. Follow her lead at meals Offer, then let her decide how much. Turning away or closing her mouth means she is done. Build on foods baby can handle, whether you began with purées, self-feeding or both. Managing soft lumps or finger foods? Adapt family food safely; keep breast milk or formula through the first year. Breastfeeding can continue after that. Eating regular meals? Update your guide ← Back to your guide Why it’s happening As she eats more food, she needs a little less milk. Eating together helps her learn by copying you. How much and how often A guide, not a target. Milk reference Nursing Breast-milk bottles Formula bottles Nursing and bottles Nursing On demand Bottles Amounts depend on how much baby nurses; follow hunger and fullness cues. Meals 3, plus 1–2 snacks Water 4–8 oz a day A day might look like: milk on waking, breakfast, lunch, snack, dinner, milk before bed. How to tell it’s enough Growth at checkups. A light-eating day is normal. What helps Adapt a family meal Set aside a portion before adding salt. Include an iron-rich food, a soft vegetable or fruit, and a starchy food; prepare each for baby’s eating skills. Plan the milk change at 12 months Whole cow’s milk can replace formula, about 16–24 oz a day from a cup. Breastfeeding can continue as long as you both want. content.question: Do I need to wake her to feed?
content.prompt: Is she back to her birth weight?
content.action: Wake her to feed every 2–3 hours, day and night, until your pediatrician says you can stop.
content.context: Most babies are back to birth weight by about 2 weeks.

content.question: Do I need to wake her to feed?
content.prompt: Is she back to her birth weight?
content.action: Ask your pediatrician if you can let her wake you for feeds.
content.context: Many babies still feed every 2–4 hours at night for a while.

content.question: Can I give her water?
content.prompt: Is it hot out?
content.action: Offer extra milk feeds instead. Babies under 6 months shouldn’t have water.
content.context: Breast milk and formula are mostly water already.

content.question: Can I give her water?
content.prompt: Is it hot out?
content.action: Not yet. Breast milk or formula covers all her fluids until about 6 months.
content.context: Small sips of water can start with solids.

content.question: Spit-up, gas or hiccups: is this normal?
content.prompt: How does she seem after feeds?
content.action: All three are common. Burp her halfway through and after feeds, and keep her upright for a bit afterward.
content.context: Spit-up usually eases by 12 months. Hiccups don’t bother most babies.

content.question: Spit-up, gas or hiccups: is this normal?
content.prompt: How does she seem after feeds?
content.action: Talk to your pediatrician. Call right away for green or forceful vomiting.
content.context: Forceful vomiting after every feed needs a same-day call.

content.question: Why is she suddenly hungrier?
content.prompt: Did it start in the last few days?
content.action: Offer milk at hunger cues and watch wet diapers and growth. A few hungrier days can happen without a new feeding stage.
content.context: Hunger alone does not show readiness for solids or establish low milk supply.

content.question: Why is she suddenly hungrier?
content.prompt: Did it start in the last few days?
content.action: Arrange a feeding review if the change persists or feeds never seem satisfying. Bring a day of feeds and wet diapers.
content.context: Steady growth is the best sign she’s getting enough.

content.question: Can she go longer at night?
content.prompt: Is she gaining well at checkups?
content.action: Ask your pediatrician if you can let her wake you rather than waking her.
content.context: Many babies still feed 1–3 times a night at this age.

content.question: Can she go longer at night?
content.prompt: Is she gaining well at checkups?
content.action: Keep the feeding plan your pediatrician gave you until the next checkup.
content.context: Night feeds help growth in the early months.

content.question: Why won’t she take a bottle?
content.prompt: Does baby take it from anyone?
content.action: Let that caregiver offer a familiar bottle while baby gets used to the change.
content.context: Try when baby is a little hungry, rather than very upset. Pause if baby turns away.

content.question: Why won’t she take a bottle?
content.prompt: Does baby take it from anyone?
content.action: Try a calm feed before baby is very hungry. Check whether the nipple flow seems hard to manage; don’t push baby to finish.
content.context: If refusal reduces usual milk intake or wet diapers, contact your pediatrician rather than waiting for the next checkup.

content.question: She seems hungrier. Should we start solids early?
content.prompt: Has your pediatrician suggested starting early?
content.action: Follow their plan, especially if early peanut was recommended for eczema.
content.context: Get set up first: high chair and a choking first-aid class.

content.question: She seems hungrier. Should we start solids early?
content.prompt: Has your pediatrician suggested starting early?
content.action: Offer more milk feeds. Hungrier days are usually a growth spurt and pass in a few days.
content.context: Most babies start solids around 6 months, once they show the readiness signs.

content.question: Purées or baby-led weaning?
content.prompt: How would you prefer to offer food?
content.action: You offer small spoonfuls and can adjust the texture yourself. This takes your help for each bite; move toward mashed and lumpier foods as baby learns.
content.context: Readiness and safe food preparation matter in every approach. Baby decides how much to eat.

content.question: Purées or baby-led weaning?
content.prompt: How would you prefer to offer food?
content.action: Baby brings prepared finger foods to their mouth. Choose this if you feel comfortable preparing safe shapes and letting baby explore, including dropped food and mess. Milk feeds continue.
content.context: Readiness and safe food preparation matter in every approach. Baby decides how much to eat.

content.question: Purées or baby-led weaning?
content.prompt: How would you prefer to offer food?
content.action: Offer some foods by spoon and some as soft finger foods, even at the same meal. You do not need to choose one approach permanently.
content.context: Readiness and safe food preparation matter in every approach. Baby decides how much to eat.

content.question: Is gagging normal?
content.prompt: Does she cough or sputter, then carry on?
content.action: That’s gagging. It’s noisy and normal while she learns. Stay calm and let her work it out.
content.context: Trouble breathing or an ineffective cough can mean choking. Know infant choking first aid.

content.question: Is gagging normal?
content.prompt: Does she cough or sputter, then carry on?
content.choice: She goes quiet or can’t breathe
content.action: That could be choking. Call 911 and start infant choking first aid.
content.context: Set up before the first bite with the feeding safety checklist.

content.question: Why is her poop different?
content.prompt: Is she straining or uncomfortable?
content.action: Offer water with meals and foods like pears, prunes, peas or oats. Ease off rice cereal and bananas for a few days.
content.context: Call your pediatrician for blood in her poop, or no poop for several days with discomfort.

content.question: Why is her poop different?
content.prompt: Is she straining or uncomfortable?
content.action: Changes in color, smell and texture are normal once solids start. What she eats often shows up.
content.context: Pale white, black or bloody poop is a reason to call.

content.question: She spits everything out. Should I stop?
content.prompt: How many times has she tried this food?
content.action: Offer a small amount again on another day, without pressure. New tastes can take repeated tries.
content.context: A surprised face is different from closing the mouth or turning away. Respect those fullness cues.

content.question: She spits everything out. Should I stop?
content.prompt: How many times has she tried this food?
content.choice: Many times, and she refuses most food
content.action: Keep meals calm and offer textures baby can manage. If most foods remain difficult or are repeatedly refused, contact your pediatrician for a feeding review.
content.context: Mention coughing, vomiting, discomfort or trouble swallowing; these need more than repeated food exposure.

content.question: Why won’t she eat lumps?
content.prompt: How does she react?
content.action: Gagging is normal while she learns. Keep offering soft lumps alongside foods she likes.
content.context: Trouble breathing or an ineffective cough can mean choking, even if there’s some sound. Know infant choking first aid.

content.question: Why won’t she eat lumps?
content.prompt: How does she react?
content.choice: Gags and vomits often, or refuses
content.action: Use a texture baby can comfortably manage and contact your pediatrician about repeated vomiting or refusal. Ask whether a feeding assessment would help.

content.question: How do milk and meals fit together?
content.prompt: How are meals going?
content.choice: Milk is going well; food varies
content.action: Keep regular milk feeds and offer meals when baby is alert and interested. Leave room between a milk feed and a meal rather than waiting until baby is very hungry.
content.context: Breast milk or infant formula remains important through the first year. Food gradually takes a bigger role.

content.question: How do milk and meals fit together?
content.prompt: How are meals going?
content.choice: Milk seems to crowd out most meals
content.action: Share milk amounts, meal opportunities and growth with your pediatrician. Agree on a balance before cutting milk feeds.
content.context: Also mention trouble swallowing or managing textures; milk is not the only possible reason for eating very little.

content.question: Can she have finger foods without teeth?
content.prompt: Can you squash the food between your fingers?
content.action: Softness matters, but shape and size matter too. Use the food-preparation guide before offering it.
content.context: Teeth don’t decide readiness. Gums are strong.

content.question: Can she have finger foods without teeth?
content.prompt: Can you squash the food between your fingers?
content.action: Cook it softer or skip it for now. Hard raw foods are a choking risk.
content.context: See the choking hazards list.

content.question: Why does appetite vary from day to day?
content.prompt: Does she eat well on some days?
content.action: That’s normal. Keep offering a mix, including one food she likes, and let her decide how much.
content.context: Over a week, it usually evens out.

content.question: Why does appetite vary from day to day?
content.prompt: Does she eat well on some days?
content.choice: She eats very little most days
content.action: Mention it at her next checkup, especially if she seems tired or isn’t growing.
content.context: Milk and food needs change at the first birthday. Review the balance at the 12-month checkup.

content.question: What’s still off-limits?
content.prompt: Is she under 12 months?
content.action: Skip honey, cow’s milk as a drink, juice, and added salt or sugar. Keep preparing choking hazards.
content.context: Whole nuts, whole grapes and popcorn stay off the menu for a few more years.

content.question: What’s still off-limits?
content.prompt: Is she under 12 months?
content.action: Whole cow’s milk can be introduced. The honey safety restriction ends at 12 months; it still counts as added sugar to avoid. Keep preparing choking hazards.
content.context: If you offer cow’s milk, discuss how it fits alongside meals and any breastfeeding.

content.question: When should she stop using bottles?
content.prompt: Is she drinking from a cup?
content.action: Start replacing one bottle a day with a cup, often the midday one first.
content.context: Most babies move off bottles between 12 and 18 months.

content.question: When should she stop using bottles?
content.prompt: Is she drinking from a cup?
content.action: Offer an open or straw cup with every meal. Practice comes before switching.
content.context: Bedtime bottles are usually the last to go.

units.content: Feeding Maya · 5 months Before the first bite Feeding safety and first aid Prepare the seat and learn first aid before starting. Revisit food preparation as textures and self-feeding change. Before the first bite 4 left Get a high chair with a harness Upright, with her feet supported if possible. Never feed her in a car seat, stroller or reclined. Learn infant choking first aid A class or the AAP video. Know what to do before you need it. Know gagging from choking Gagging can happen while learning to eat. Trouble breathing or a weak or absent cough can mean choking, even if there’s some sound. Call 911 and use infant choking first aid you’ve learned. Have a soft spoon and an open cup Small, soft-tipped spoons, and a cup for sips of water from 6 months. Once baby is eating Choking hazards Whole nuts, whole grapes, popcorn, round slices of hot dog, raw carrot or apple, and spoonfuls of thick nut butter. Make it safe Quarter grapes lengthwise, cook vegetables until soft, thin nut butter, and cut food into finger-sized strips. Foods and drinks to wait on No honey or cow’s milk as a drink before 12 months. Avoid juice before 12 months and added sugars before age 2; limit added salt. Keep in mind Stay with her and keep her sitting upright for every meal and snack. Based on AAP and CDC guidance.

Feeding Maya · 5 months Your milk reference Breast milk and formula basics Store, prepare and offer milk safely. Follow any feeding plan your pediatrician has given you. Spit-up, gas or hiccups: is this normal? ＋ How does she seem after feeds? Happy and growing Upset, arching or not gaining The essentials Breast milk storage · CDC Room temperature: up to 4 hours. Fridge: up to 4 days. Freezer: within 6 months is best; up to 12 months is acceptable. Use refrigerated thawed milk within 24 hours after it is fully thawed; don’t refreeze fully thawed milk. Making formula · Follow the label Measure exactly as the label says. Never water it down or add extra powder. Use prepared formula within 2 hours, or 1 hour once a feed starts. Pumping and bottles · If you express milk While you’re apart or exclusively pumping, pump about as often as baby feeds. If you also nurse, introducing bottles can take practice; another caregiver can try a calm feed. Choosing formula · For most babies Standard iron-fortified infant formula, including store brands, suits most babies. If baby has a prescribed formula or feeding plan for early birth, growth or allergy concerns, check before changing it. Warming bottles · Optional Babies don’t need warm milk. If you warm it, use warm water, not a microwave, and test a few drops on your wrist. Vitamin D · Ask your pediatrician Under 12 months, babies need 400 IU a day. Breastfed and partly breastfed babies need daily drops; formula-fed babies may too if intake is below about 32 oz a day. From age one, the daily need is 600 IU. Ask your pediatrician which supplement fits. Every bottle Wash your hands before making a bottle, and clean bottles after every feed. Hold her semi-upright and pace the feed; pause every few minutes. Never prop a bottle or put her to bed with one. Formula: discard leftovers within 1 hour of starting the feed. Breast milk: use leftovers within 2 hours after the feed ends, then discard. Sources behind this guide ＋ CDC · Breast milk storage ↗ CDC · Formula preparation and storage ↗ CDC · Vitamin D ↗ AAP · Spit-up and reflux ↗

Feeding Maya · 5 months Starting solids · Usually around 6 months Introducing allergens Introducing peanut and well-cooked egg alongside other first foods may help prevent those allergies. The common ones Peanut, egg, cow’s milk, wheat, soy, sesame, tree nuts, fish and shellfish. How to start Start once she is eating other solids, around 6 months. Offer one new allergen at a time, a small amount, early in the day. Use a safe form: peanut butter thinned into purée, well-cooked egg. Never whole nuts. Once she tolerates it, keep it in her diet a few times a week. If baby reacts Mild A few hives around her mouth: stop the food and call your pediatrician. Serious Trouble breathing, swelling of lips or tongue, repeated vomiting, or she is limp or pale: call 911. Before you start Ask your pediatrician first if she has severe eczema or an egg allergy. Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Starting solid foods ↗ AAP · Introducing allergens ↗ Based on NIAID and AAP guidance.

Feeding Maya · 5 months Feeding When to ask for feeding help How to tell Normal Effortless spit-up in a happy, growing baby. Cluster feeding for a few days. Gagging while learning to eat. Appetite that swings day to day. Keep an eye on it Changes in feeding length or appetite: note intake, wet diapers and how baby seems. A shorter feed alone does not show how much milk baby took.. Call your pediatrician if Fewer wet diapers than usual. Not back to birth weight by 2 weeks. Repeated vomiting or refusal with textures. Little interest in food after 9 months. Reduced milk intake or repeated feed refusal. Hives or vomiting after a new food. Blood in baby’s stool. Call 911 if Trouble breathing or swelling of lips or tongue after a food. Choking that doesn’t clear. She is limp or won’t wake. For you Feeding is hard work If nursing hurts or feeding feels overwhelming, a lactation consultant can help, and is often covered by insurance. Asking for help is normal. Before a visit, note a day of feeds and wet diapers. It helps your pediatrician see the pattern.

Sleep Maya · 5 months Your approach · Optional Settling and sleep training Choose the guidance you need. Helping baby fall asleep can remain part of your routine. What would help right now? Compare sleep-training methods Support while trying sleep training Keep a routine working Settle with my help Sleep training is optional and is usually considered from 4–6 months. Ask your pediatrician about readiness, especially after early birth or with feeding or growth concerns. Ferber Return for check-ins Return for brief reassurance at planned intervals. Check-ins can reassure some babies and unsettle others; some crying is expected. More about Ferber Cleveland Clinic · Free ↗ Chair method Stay nearby, then step back Sit beside the crib, then gradually move farther away over time. Keeps you nearby, but can take patience. More about the chair method Cleveland Clinic · Free ↗ Pick up, put down Comfort, then return to the crib Pick up to soothe, then put baby back before sleep. Repeated lifting can take time and energy. More about pick up, put down Cleveland Clinic · Free ↗ Cry it out Settle without routine check-ins Allow settling without routine soothing visits, while staying alert to baby’s needs. Can involve crying without reassurance. More about cry it out Cleveland Clinic · Free ↗ Bedtime fading Move bedtime gradually Start close to the time baby usually falls asleep, then gradually bring bedtime earlier as settling gets easier. Aims to reduce time awake in bed. Research on bedtime fading Pediatrics · Study abstract ↗ 1 / 5 ‹ Previous Next › Before you start ＋ Choose a response you can repeat Think about how much hands-on soothing you want to offer and what each caregiver can sustain. Keep needed night feeds Choose how to respond between feeds. Learning to settle does not mean baby no longer needs to eat. Know when to pause Respond to illness, discomfort and hunger. If the approach feels unmanageable, stop and review the plan rather than pushing through. Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Settling and nighttime needs ↗ Cleveland Clinic · Timing and approaches ↗

Sleep Maya · 5 months Your approach · Optional Settling and sleep training Choose the guidance you need. Helping baby fall asleep can remain part of your routine. What would help right now? Compare sleep-training methods Support while trying sleep training Keep a routine working Settle with my help Look for progress in settling Compare a few nights Is baby taking less time to settle or needing less help? A needed night feed can still be part of progress. After a difficult night Respond to hunger, discomfort or illness. Once those needs are met, use your chosen settling response. One rough night does not call for a new method. If it isn’t getting easier Pause if settling is not improving or the response feels hard to sustain. Bring a few nights of bedtime, wakes and feeds to your pediatrician to review what may be getting in the way. Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Settling and nighttime needs ↗ Cleveland Clinic · Timing and approaches ↗

Sleep Maya · 5 months Your approach · Optional Settling and sleep training Choose the guidance you need. Helping baby fall asleep can remain part of your routine. What would help right now? Compare sleep-training methods Support while trying sleep training Keep a routine working Settle with my help Keep what works When naps change If naps are short and baby is tired again, keep offering the extra sleep. Don’t drop a nap just because bedtime has improved. After illness or travel Offer the comfort baby needs during the disruption. When it passes, return to familiar bedtime steps and adjust timing around the day’s naps. If sleep stays difficult Notice whether the problem is falling asleep, waking between feeds or staying asleep. Discuss a persistent change, especially with discomfort, feeding or growth concerns. Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Settling and nighttime needs ↗ Cleveland Clinic · Timing and approaches ↗

Sleep Maya · 5 months Your approach · Optional Settling and sleep training Choose the guidance you need. Helping baby fall asleep can remain part of your routine. What would help right now? Compare sleep-training methods Support while trying sleep training Keep a routine working Settle with my help Build a routine around your help Keep the lead-in familiar Use a short sequence you can repeat: a feed, diaper change, then a quiet song or book. Feeding, rocking or holding to sleep can remain part of it. Make it repeatable for another caregiver Show them the same steps and the soothing baby responds to. They can offer comfort their own way while keeping familiar cues. If settling is taking longer Check hunger, discomfort and whether the last nap changed. Adjust bedtime to tiredness before adding more steps to the routine. Sources behind this guide ＋ AAP · Settling and nighttime needs ↗ Cleveland Clinic · Timing and approaches ↗

content.title: Check the car-seat fit and installation
content.reason: The seat’s fit and installation are details you can get hands-on help with.
content.action: A certified technician can check the installation and show you the harness fit.
content.instructions: For a rear-facing seat, harness straps sit at or below baby’s shoulders, and you can’t pinch any slack at the shoulder. The chest clip sits at armpit level. Follow your seat and vehicle manuals.

content.title: Make your changing spot fall-safe
content.reason: A new roll can happen while you reach for a clean diaper.
content.action: Keep supplies within arm’s reach so one hand can stay on baby. A mat on the floor, away from hazards, removes the risk of falling from a changing table.
content.instructions: On a raised surface, keep a hand on baby and never step away, even for a second. A strap doesn’t replace staying with them.

content.title: Clear beyond the play mat
content.reason: The play mat’s edge won’t stop a roll.
content.action: Leave clear floor around the mat: check nearby furniture edges, cords and small objects.
content.instructions: A roll can carry baby off the mat. Use a firm floor-level play surface; avoid beds and sofas for rolling practice.

content.title: Secure button batteries
content.reason: Small devices beside the play space can be picked up and mouthed.
content.action: Check remotes, key fobs, musical cards and toys for secure battery covers. Store spare and used batteries, and small battery devices, out of reach.
content.instructions: Check the compartment itself, including on musical books and greeting cards. A cover that comes loose leaves the battery accessible.

content.title: Give visitors’ bags a place out of reach
content.reason: A visitor’s bag can bring medicines into baby’s new reach.
content.action: Purses and backpacks often hold medicines. Keep them up high, not on the floor or a low chair.
content.instructions: Child-resistant caps are not childproof. Use locked storage for household medicines, and keep visitors’ bags out of reach.

content.title: Check for small parts at floor level
content.action: Look for coins, magnets and pieces from older children’s toys where baby plays.
content.instructions: As a quick check, keep objects that fit inside an empty toilet-paper tube out of reach. Larger objects can still be unsafe. Recheck after visitors, crafts or older children’s play.

content.title: Fit the right stair gates
content.reason: Moving across the floor gives baby access to spaces beyond the play mat.
content.action: Gate the top and bottom of stairs. At the top, use a gate screwed into the wall, not a pressure-mounted or pet gate.
content.instructions: Use a gate made for children and follow its instructions. Check doorways into rooms baby shouldn’t enter, too.

content.title: Anchor furniture and TVs
content.reason: Pulling against a dresser, bookcase or TV stand can tip it.
content.action: Secure dressers, bookcases and TVs before baby uses them as handholds.
content.instructions: Use anti-tip hardware suited to your furniture and wall. Follow the hardware and furniture instructions; the guide shows how to attach and check it.

content.title: Lock away medicines and cleaning products
content.reason: Cupboard contents become reachable once baby can travel across the room.
content.action: Lock away cleaners, detergent pods, medicines, vitamins and supplements, even in child-resistant packaging.
content.instructions: Relock after each use and pull the door to check it holds.

content.title: Cover outlets and move cords
content.action: Use outlet covers baby can’t pull out, and move cords out of reach.
content.instructions: Choose covers baby cannot remove and that are too large to choke on. If replacing outlets, use tamper-resistant ones.

content.title: Check window access
content.reason: A new standing or climbing height can bring a window within reach.
content.action: Move furniture baby could climb away from windows. Screens don’t stop falls.
content.instructions: Use window stops or guards to limit openings and gaps to 4 inches or less. Keep at least one window in each room usable by an adult for escape in a fire.

content.title: Go cordless on window coverings
content.reason: Cords out of reach from the floor may be reachable from furniture.
content.action: Choose cordless blinds or shades. Check for cords reachable from the floor and from furniture.
content.instructions: Inner cords and loops can be reachable even when the pull cord is tied up.

content.title: Keep bathrooms and other risky rooms closed off
content.action: Use suitable latches, knob covers or gates to block access to bathrooms, the laundry room and garage.
content.instructions: Choose devices adults can open quickly in an emergency. Check toilet and water access; consider a toilet-lid lock. Relatch doors after use.

content.title: Check the hot-water setting
content.action: Set the water heater to 120°F or lower.
content.instructions: Follow the heater instructions, or ask a plumber or your landlord. Check bath water and stay within reach; a lower setting does not replace supervision. Anti-scald devices add protection at taps.

content.title: Check smoke and carbon monoxide alarms
content.action: Test each alarm and check placement, including the areas around baby’s bedroom.
content.instructions: Smoke alarms belong on every level, inside bedrooms and outside sleeping areas. Put CO alarms near sleeping areas and follow manufacturer instructions for testing and replacement.

content.title: Secure pool or spa access
content.action: Use barriers and self-closing, self-latching gates that separate children from the water.
content.instructions: Check doors leading outside too, and close gates after every use. Barriers don’t replace watching baby near water.

content.title: Skip seated walkers with wheels
content.action: They let baby move fast and reach hazards, and they don’t help with walking.
content.instructions: Choose floor play or a stationary activity center instead. This advice is about seated walkers with wheels; push-along toys are a different product.
